metadata.title: WHO recommendations on the assessment of postpartum blood loss and use of a treatment bundle for postpartum haemorrhage
metadata.summary: The guideline addresses objective measurement of blood loss after birth to improve detection and prompt treatment of postpartum haemorrhage. It also recommends a timely, standardized approach combining blood loss assessment with a first-line treatment bundle and an implementation strategy for women having a vaginal birth. It discusses implementation across care settings and notes that further research is needed before bundle care can be confidently recommended for caesarean section births.

therapeutic_areas: objective measurement of postpartum blood loss

prophylaxis.recommendation: WHO recommends monitoring coverage of prophylactic uterotonics as a process indicator for PPH monitoring and prevention. Calculate coverage by dividing the number of women who receive prophylactic uterotonics during the third stage of labour by the number of all women giving birth.

conditions.name: postpartum haemorrhage
conditions.description: Bleeding after childbirth that requires prompt recognition and treatment. In the outcomes considered by the guideline, PPH is identified at blood loss ≥ 500 ml.
conditions.epidemiology: WHO estimates that about 14 million women experience PPH each year. Obstetric haemorrhage accounts for 27% of maternal deaths worldwide each year, and most of those deaths are due to PPH.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Excessive postpartum blood loss may be accompanied by early warning signs such as tachycardia or hypotension.

diagnostic_workup.test: Objective measurement of postpartum blood loss
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect PPH and enable prompt treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Routinely for all women giving birth; measurement is particularly important during the first few hours after birth.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline uses blood loss ≥ 500 ml to identify PPH among its priority outcomes. In a large trial, the treatment bundle was initiated at measured blood loss of 500 ml or greater, or 300 ml or greater when early warning signs of excessive blood loss were present; these trial triggers do not replace clinical judgement.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For women having a vaginal birth.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Most available evidence on measurement after vaginal birth concerns calibrated drapes. Objective quantification is more likely to detect PPH than visual estimation, which is frequently inaccurate.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recognize early signs of excessive blood loss.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Regularly after birth, particularly during the first few hours.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Tachycardia and hypotension are examples of early warning signs. The outcomes considered also include changes in heart rate, blood pressure and urine output.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: As part of the first-line PPH treatment bundle.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess postpartum anaemia and the change in concentration before and after delivery among the outcomes considered by the guideline.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Postpartum anaemia is defined among the priority outcomes as a haemoglobin (Hb) lower than 9 mg/dl.

follow_up.schedule: Monitor regularly after birth, with particular attention to blood loss during the first few hours.
recommended_tests: Monitoring for early warning signs of excessive blood loss, including tachycardia and hypotension

conditions.name: severe PPH
conditions.description: The severe category of postpartum haemorrhage is defined in the guideline’s priority outcomes by blood loss ≥ 1000 ml.

diagnostic_workup.test: Objective measurement of postpartum blood loss
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Severe PPH is defined among the priority outcomes as blood loss ≥ 1000 ml.

conditions.name: refractory postpartum bleeding
conditions.description: Postpartum bleeding that persists after the woman has received every intervention in the PPH treatment bundle.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Continued bleeding despite completion of the PPH treatment bundle.

recommendations.statement: Routinely measure blood loss after birth using an objective method for all women giving birth, to enable earlier detection and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage. A calibrated drape is one option for vaginal births.
recommendations.context: Measurement is especially important during the first few hours after birth and should be linked to a standardized, promptly initiated treatment approach. The available studies involved vaginal births, although measuring blood loss during caesarean section is also clinically important.
recommendations.rationale: Visual estimates are often inaccurate and can delay recognition of postpartum haemorrhage; objective measurement is more likely to detect it.

recommendations.statement: For all women having a vaginal birth, use a timely, standardized approach to postpartum haemorrhage management that combines objective blood loss assessment with a treatment bundle supported by an implementation strategy. First-line bundle care should promptly include uterine massage, an oxytocic agent, tranexamic acid, intravenous fluids, genital tract examination and escalation of care.
recommendations.context: The bundle interventions should ideally begin within the first 15 minutes after a postpartum haemorrhage diagnosis. If some components are unavailable, those available should still be started promptly and systematically. Continued bleeding after the complete bundle requires prompt escalation. Evidence for the bundle comes largely from vaginal births; further research is needed before bundle care can be confidently recommended for caesarean section births.
recommendations.rationale: A large trial found a 60% reduction in its composite primary outcome of severe postpartum haemorrhage, laparotomy or maternal death from postpartum haemorrhage with a combined detection, treatment-bundle and implementation intervention. The benefit cannot be assigned to an individual component.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: All women giving birth, including women undergoing a caesarean section.
decision_rules: Measure postpartum blood loss objectively as a routine practice to support early recognition and prompt treatment of PPH.
For vaginal births, calibrated drapes are one way to quantify blood loss objectively.
Link blood loss measurement to a standardized treatment protocol; identification without prompt treatment is unlikely to improve maternal outcomes.
Regularly assess for early signs of excessive bleeding, including tachycardia or hypotension.

recommended_regimens.name: Routine objective measurement of postpartum blood loss
recommended_regimens.summary: Quantify blood loss after birth for every woman to improve recognition of PPH and enable timely treatment. Most evidence for calibrated drapes concerns vaginal births, although measuring blood loss during caesarean section is also clinically important.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Measurement is especially important during the first few hours after birth.

response_assessment.timepoint: The first few hours after birth
response_assessment.method: Objective measurement of blood loss alongside regular monitoring for early warning signs of excessive bleeding.
response_assessment.interpretation: Measured blood loss and clinical findings should inform prompt initiation of a standardized PPH treatment approach.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Visual estimation is often inaccurate and may delay recognition of PPH. Blood loss measurement should preserve women’s customary and cultural preferences, including their chosen birth position. Discuss bleeding risks and signs of excessive blood loss with women throughout the birth continuum, including antenatally, to support shared decisions.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women having a vaginal birth who experience PPH.
decision_rules: Use clinical judgement when deciding to initiate PPH treatment. In a large trial, the bundle was started at measured blood loss of 500 ml or greater, or at 300 ml or greater when early warning signs of excessive blood loss were present; these are trial criteria, not a stated universal treatment threshold.
Combine early objective detection with a standardized, timely treatment bundle and an implementation strategy.
Start all bundle interventions ideally within the first 15 minutes after PPH diagnosis.
If some interventions are unavailable, begin the available components promptly and in a standardized manner.

recommended_regimens.name: PPH treatment bundle
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide rapid uterine massage, an oxytocic agent, tranexamic acid and intravenous fluids, examine the genital tract, and escalate care. Objective blood loss assessment and an implementation strategy form part of the recommended standardized approach.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The E-MOTIVE trial, involving over 200 000 study participants, reported a 60% reduction in its composite primary outcome of severe PPH, laparotomy or maternal death from PPH with a complex intervention combining PPH detection, a treatment bundle and an implementation strategy. The benefit cannot be assigned to an individual component.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: All bundle treatment interventions should ideally be initiated within the first 15 minutes after a diagnosis of PPH.

alternative_regimens.name: Available components of the PPH treatment bundle
alternative_regimens.summary: Initiate whichever bundle interventions are available without delay and in a standardized manner.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Not all bundle interventions are available in the care setting.

response_assessment.timepoint: After initiation of the PPH treatment bundle
response_assessment.method: Assess whether postpartum bleeding continues after all bundle interventions have been given.
response_assessment.interpretation: Continued bleeding despite all bundle interventions constitutes refractory postpartum bleeding and calls for prompt escalation.

supportive_care: Ensure adequate staffing, training and access to the medicines and equipment needed for coordinated treatment.
Use appropriately stocked PPH trolleys or carry cases where the implementation strategy includes them.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence for the bundle comes largely from vaginal births in secondary-level facilities. The trial’s implementation support included audit and feedback, facility champions, restocking of treatment supplies and health-worker training. Prompt recognition and treatment are also relevant in primary care, community and home settings, where resources, training and implementation strategies should be adapted to the setting. Engage women and their communities in decisions about treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women who continue to bleed after receiving every intervention in the PPH treatment bundle.
decision_rules: If postpartum bleeding persists despite completion of the treatment bundle, promptly escalate to a higher-level health-care facility or to a senior clinical provider able to provide further management.

recommended_regimens.name: Prompt escalation of care
recommended_regimens.summary: Arrange immediate access to higher-level or senior clinical management for refractory postpartum bleeding. This document does not specify the subsequent treatment regimen.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document points to separate WHO recommendations for treatment of refractory PPH.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women undergoing a caesarean section who experience PPH.
decision_rules: Measure postpartum blood loss objectively; the document considers this clinically important during caesarean section.

Distinguish the individual PPH interventions recommended by WHO for caesarean section from a treatment bundle: the document does not make a confident recommendation for bundle care in this population.

recommended_regimens.name: Individual PPH treatment interventions
recommended_regimens.summary: The document states that WHO also recommends the individual interventions contained in the PPH treatment bundle for women undergoing a caesarean section, referring to its 2012 guidance. It does not establish the bundle itself as a recommended caesarean-section pathway.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence supporting the bundle comes largely from vaginal births. The group found no clear evidence to rule out the possibility that the findings would differ for caesarean section, and stated that more research is needed before bundle care can be confidently recommended for caesarean-section births.

therapies_index.name: PPH treatment bundle
approved_indications: First-line treatment of PPH in women following vaginal birth.
therapies_index.administration: Use the components in a standardized, timely manner, ideally starting all treatment interventions within the first 15 minutes after PPH is diagnosed. If some components are unavailable, initiate those available without delay.
monitoring: Continue assessing bleeding; persistent bleeding despite all bundle interventions requires prompt escalation to a higher-level health-care facility or a senior clinical provider.

therapies_index.name: uterine massage
approved_indications: First-line treatment of PPH as part of the PPH treatment bundle.
therapies_index.administration: Begin rapidly after PPH is diagnosed.

therapies_index.name: oxytocic agent
approved_indications: First-line treatment of PPH as part of the PPH treatment bundle.
therapies_index.administration: Administer promptly as a component of the PPH treatment bundle; the guideline does not specify an agent-specific route or dose.

therapies_index.name: tranexamic acid
approved_indications: Treatment of PPH, including as part of the first-line PPH treatment bundle.
therapies_index.administration: Avoid intrathecal administration and do not mix with oxytocin before administration because some tranexamic acid products may interact with it.

therapies_index.name: intravenous fluids
approved_indications: First-line treatment of PPH as part of the PPH treatment bundle.
therapies_index.administration: Give intravenously as part of the timely PPH treatment bundle; no fluid type or volume is specified.

therapies_index.name: examination of the genital tract
approved_indications: First-line management of PPH as part of the PPH treatment bundle.
therapies_index.administration: Undertake promptly as a component of the PPH treatment bundle.

therapies_index.name: escalation of care
approved_indications: Management of PPH as part of the first-line treatment bundle.
Refractory postpartum bleeding after all PPH treatment bundle interventions have been given.
therapies_index.administration: For refractory bleeding, promptly involve a senior clinical provider able to provide further management or transfer to a higher-level health-care facility.

therapies_index.name: uterotonics
approved_indications: Prevention of PPH when used prophylactically.
Treatment of PPH when used therapeutically.
therapies_index.administration: Use the correct dosage and prevent use for other indications; no specific dose or route is provided here.

special_populations.considerations: Most evidence for objective postpartum blood loss measurement comes from studies using calibrated drapes after vaginal birth. The evidence supporting a standardized approach to detecting and treating postpartum haemorrhage, including a treatment bundle, also largely concerns vaginal births.

Measuring blood loss is clinically important after a caesarean section, although the available studies of measurement methods involved vaginal births. WHO also recommends the individual interventions in the postpartum haemorrhage treatment bundle for caesarean births, but the group considered further research necessary before it could confidently recommend bundle care for this population.

special_populations.population: Women giving birth in primary care settings, in the community or at home
special_populations.considerations: Prompt recognition and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage remain relevant in these settings, although most supporting evidence comes from secondary-level health-care facilities. Implementation requires suitable resources, health worker training and strategies tailored to the setting.
Bleeding is refractory when it continues despite receipt of every intervention in the postpartum haemorrhage treatment bundle.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Promptly escalate care to a higher-level health-care facility or a senior clinical provider able to provide further management.

special_populations.considerations: Adaptation of the recommendations should take account of these women’s particular needs, values and preferences, and should align with other emergency response strategies. Tools tailored to the context may be needed.

special_populations.population: Women with customary or cultural requirements during birth
special_populations.considerations: Postpartum blood loss measurement should preserve customary or cultural requirements, including the woman’s chosen birth position.

artifacts.title: Table 1. Summary of recommendations and remarks

rows: Recommendation 1 — Recommended. Routinely measure postpartum blood loss objectively in every woman giving birth to improve recognition and prompt treatment of postpartum haemorrhage. A calibrated drape is one way to quantify loss objectively after vaginal birth.

Recommendation 2 — Recommended. For every woman having a vaginal birth, use a timely, standardized approach to PPH management that combines objective blood-loss assessment with a treatment bundle and an implementation strategy. First-line bundle components are rapid uterine massage, an oxytocic agent, tranexamic acid, intravenous fluids, genital tract examination and escalation of care.

Remarks — Assessment of postpartum blood loss: Visual estimates are often inaccurate and can delay or miss PPH recognition; objective quantification is more likely to identify it. Most evidence after vaginal birth concerns calibrated drapes. Measurement is especially important in the first few hours after birth, alongside regular checks for early signs such as tachycardia or hypotension. Blood-loss measurement and a standardized, promptly initiated treatment protocol must be linked; identification without prompt treatment is unlikely to improve outcomes. Although studies involved vaginal births, measuring loss during caesarean section is also clinically important. Measurement practices should preserve customary and cultural needs, including preferred birth position. Discuss bleeding risks and warning signs with women throughout the birth continuum, including antenatally, to support shared decisions. Consider investment in sustainable, climate-friendly drapes.

Remarks — Care bundle for the treatment of PPH: The bundle’s individual interventions were recommended in the existing 2012 and 2017 WHO PPH guidelines; here, “bundle” means a clinical care bundle for PPH treatment. Early PPH detection is integral to the first response, and most measurement evidence concerns calibrated drapes after vaginal birth. Clinical judgement guides treatment: in a large trial, the bundle began at measured loss of 500 ml or greater, or 300 ml or greater when early warning signs were present. Trial implementation measures included adequate staffing, dedicated research staff, facility audit and feedback, designated champions, restocked PPH trolleys or carry cases, and health-worker training. Ideally, begin every bundle intervention within the first 15 minutes after PPH diagnosis; if some components are unavailable, initiate those available promptly and consistently. Continued bleeding after all bundle interventions requires prompt escalation to a higher-level facility or a senior provider able to manage it. Bundle evidence comes largely from vaginal-birth trials: individual interventions are also recommended for caesarean births, but more research is needed before bundle care can be confidently recommended for caesarean births. Sustainable implementation requires strengthened health systems, adequate staff and commodities. Although most supporting studies were in secondary-level facilities, prompt recognition and treatment also matter in primary care, community and home settings, with suitable resources, training and setting-specific implementation. Engage women and communities to uphold women’s rights, agency and shared treatment decisions.

document_sections.heading: Executive summary
document_sections.content: The GDG made two recommendations: one on objectively assessing postpartum blood loss and another on promptly managing PPH with a treatment bundle and an implementation strategy. Its accompanying remarks explain how to apply them.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Global estimates put maternal deaths at 287 000 in 2020, predominantly in the least developed countries; 87% occurred in sub-Saharan African and South Asian countries. Obstetric haemorrhage accounts for 27% of maternal deaths worldwide each year, and most of those deaths result from PPH. WHO estimates that about 14 million women experience PPH annually. Better prevention and treatment of PPH could substantially reduce maternal illness and death and contribute to the SDGs. Health workers, particularly where the burden is greatest, need current evidence, training and access to effective interventions. In March 2023, WHO brought together over 130 stakeholders to identify priorities for preventing avoidable PPH deaths between 2023 and 2030. A trial published in May 2023 included over 200 000 participants and reported a 60% reduction in its combined primary outcome of severe PPH, laparotomy or maternal death from PPH. Because that trial combined detection, treatment and implementation measures, its benefit cannot be assigned to any single component. WHO therefore reviewed both treatment-bundle evidence and the evidence behind its 2012 position on assessing postpartum blood loss.

document_sections.heading: What’s new?
document_sections.content: In 2012, WHO found insufficient evidence to favour measured over clinically estimated blood loss in the third stage of labour: studies comparing calibrated drapes alone with visual estimation alone had shown no clear effect on PPH-related outcomes. WHO had not previously recommended a PPH treatment bundle. Its 2023 review led to two recommendations favouring objective postpartum blood-loss measurement and, for vaginal births, prompt standardized PPH management that combines such measurement with a treatment bundle and an implementation strategy.

document_sections.heading: Target audience
document_sections.content: The recommendations primarily address people developing health-care policies and protocols, maternal and child health programme managers, and policy-makers in every setting. They also serve obstetricians, midwives, nurses, general practitioners and others caring directly for women giving birth. The guidance can inform clinical training tools and efforts to strengthen health services.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation development methods
document_sections.content: Development followed the WHO handbook for guideline development: priority questions and outcomes were selected, evidence was retrieved and assessed, recommendations were formulated, and dissemination, implementation, evaluation and updating were planned. Updated and new systematic reviews informed the evidence profiles. Quantitative evidence was assessed with GRADE and qualitative evidence with GRADE-CERQual. The GDG used GRADE EtD frameworks addressing effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability and feasibility, and met on 31 August and 1 September 2023.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations
document_sections.content: The GDG issued one recommendation about assessing postpartum blood loss and another about treatment bundles. Table 1 brings together both recommendations and their implementation remarks; the accompanying remarks in section 3.1 are intended to guide interpretation.

document_sections.heading: 1 Introduction
document_sections.content: This chapter explains the burden of PPH, why WHO revisited its earlier position on blood-loss assessment, the populations and audiences addressed, and the questions concerning detection and treatment that guided the recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 1.1Background
document_sections.content: An estimated 287 000 maternal deaths occurred in 2020, mostly in the least developed countries; 87% occurred in sub-Saharan African and South Asian countries. Obstetric haemorrhage causes 27% of maternal deaths globally each year, predominantly through PPH, which WHO estimates affects about 14 million women annually. Reducing PPH could lessen maternal mortality and morbidity and advance the SDGs and WHO’s health-coverage goals. Women, including adolescents, have a right to evidence-based pregnancy and childbirth care. Health workers need current evidence, suitable interventions and training, while managers and policy-makers need guidance for service planning. Care that is accessible, acceptable and of high quality could help address global inequities in maternal and newborn outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 1.2Rationale and objectives
document_sections.content: Since 2017, WHO has used a living-guidelines process to review new evidence across more than 400 MPH recommendations. That process supported rapid guidance on tranexamic acid treatment in 2017 and updated uterotonic prevention guidance in 2018 after large multinational trials. A WHO consultation in 2017 proposed both a first-line PPH treatment bundle and a bundle for PPH unresponsive to initial treatment, while acknowledging insufficient direct evidence about bundle outcomes. In March 2023, over 130 participants at the PPH Summit considered priorities for ending preventable PPH deaths between 2023 and 2030 and noted the potential importance of the E-MOTIVE trial. Published in May 2023, that trial involved over 200 000 participants and reported a 60% reduction in its composite primary outcome of severe PPH, laparotomy or maternal death from PPH. Care bundles are small groups of evidence-based practices, generally three to five, intended to be delivered together and reliably. The trial tested PPH detection, bundled treatment and an implementation strategy as one complex intervention, so its observed benefit cannot be attributed to an individual element. This prompted reconsideration of blood-loss assessment as well as bundle treatment. WHO’s 2012 conclusion had found insufficient evidence to favour blood-loss measurement over clinical estimation; the advice in this document replaces that conclusion. Recommendations were prepared under WHO guideline procedures using evidence synthesis, GRADE and GDG deliberation.

document_sections.heading: 1.3Target audience
document_sections.content: WHO MPH guidance concerns care during pregnancy, labour, childbirth and the postpartum period in any setting. These recommendations principally serve policy and protocol developers, midwives, nurses, general medical practitioners, obstetricians and maternal and child health programme managers. Professional societies, organizations promoting woman-centred maternity care and programme implementers may also use them.

document_sections.heading: 1.4Scope of the recommendations
document_sections.content: The guidance addresses PPH detection and treatment. Its first PICO question asks whether, from the third stage of labour until 24 hours after delivery, particular blood-loss assessment methods improve PPH detection and maternal and perinatal outcomes compared with other methods. Its second asks whether, among women with PPH, a care bundle improves maternal and perinatal outcomes compared with usual care or a bundle with different components.

document_sections.heading: 1.5Persons affected by the recommendations
document_sections.content: The recommendations affect women giving birth and women experiencing PPH in low-, middle- and high-resource settings.

document_sections.heading: 2 Methods
document_sections.content: WHO followed its guideline-development procedures, moving from priority questions and evidence retrieval through evidence appraisal and recommendation formulation to plans for dissemination, implementation, evaluation and updates. In 2023, recommendations on PPH detection and bundle treatment were identified as a priority.

document_sections.heading: 2.1Contributors to the guideline
document_sections.content: Six groups contributed to developing the recommendations. WHO staff coordinated the update; external experts and affected-population representatives formulated recommendations; evidence specialists prepared reviews and appraisal; observers and an external review group contributed implementation perspectives and document review.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.1 WHO Steering Group
document_sections.content: WHO staff from SRH and MCA coordinated the update. They framed PICO questions, selected review and guideline teams, supervised evidence synthesis, organized GDG deliberations and prepared the final document and implementation plans.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.2 Guideline Development Group (GDG)
document_sections.content: The GDG brought together clinical, research, policy, programme, methodological and affected-population perspectives on intrapartum and immediate postpartum care. Of a wider pool of approximately 50 experts and stakeholders, 15 were invited, with attention to geographical and gender representation and conflicts of interest. After appraising and interpreting the evidence, the GDG formulated the recommendations at meetings on 31 August and 1 September 2023 and approved the final document.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.3 Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG)
document_sections.content: The ESG conducted or updated systematic reviews, appraised evidence and assembled EtD frameworks. Its work included a qualitative review of PPH prevention, detection and management and a new review of economic evaluations. ESG members presented synthesized findings and addressed technical questions during GDG deliberations.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.4 External partners and observers
document_sections.content: Representatives of organizations involved in disseminating or implementing maternal-health guidance attended GDG meetings as observers.

document_sections.heading: 2.1.5 External Review Group (ERG)
document_sections.content: Six technical experts from five WHO regions reviewed factual accuracy, clarity, context and implementation implications, including whether relevant values and preferences had informed decisions. Their remit did not include changing GDG recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 2.2Evidence identification and retrieval
document_sections.content: Systematic review teams and the WHO Steering Group gathered evidence on intervention effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, experiences and preferences, resource use, and cost–effectiveness.

document_sections.heading: 2.2.1 Evidence on effectiveness
document_sections.content: WHO commissioned an update of a systematic review on postpartum blood-loss assessment and a new systematic review of PPH treatment-bundle effectiveness.

document_sections.heading: Methods to assess postpartum blood loss for the detection of PPH
document_sections.content: An updated randomized-trial review, last published in 2018, searched on 14 June 2023. The earlier review contained three trials, two contributing data; the update contained four trials, three contributing data. Additional data did not alter estimated effects or their certainty for priority outcomes. A rapid diagnostic-accuracy review searched references from seven systematic reviews and structured MEDLINE results. Studies comparing any two assessment methods qualified if they reported diagnostic measures for PPH of 500 ml or more or severe PPH of 1000 ml or more. Findings from eight eligible studies were reported.

document_sections.heading: Effectiveness of care bundles in the treatment of PPH
document_sections.content: Reviewers prepared an agreed protocol covering PICO criteria, searches, bias assessment and analysis. Searches of six databases had no date or language restriction and considered studies from countries at all income levels and in any care setting. Eligible designs included randomized and non-randomized trials, interrupted time series and controlled or uncontrolled before–after studies. A potentially eligible bundle combined three or more interventions delivered concurrently or collectively. For these recommendations, the question of interest was treatment rather than prevention of PPH.

document_sections.heading: 2.2.2 Evidence on values, equity, acceptability and feasibility, and resource use and cost–effectiveness
document_sections.content: Qualitative and economic reviews supplied evidence beyond clinical effectiveness for GDG consideration.

document_sections.heading: Values, equity, acceptability and feasibility
document_sections.content: A 2023 qualitative evidence synthesis examined experiences and views of women, community members, lay health workers and skilled health workers concerning PPH or its prevention, detection and management in communities and facilities. It was the principal source for judgments about equity, feasibility and acceptability.

document_sections.heading: Resource use and cost–effectiveness
document_sections.content: A new systematic review examined economic evidence for preventing, diagnosing and treating PPH. Eligible full evaluations assessed cost–benefit, cost–effectiveness or cost–utility. For these recommendations, only evaluations of blood-loss measurement and PPH treatment bundles were used.

document_sections.heading: 2.3Quality assessment and grading of the evidence
document_sections.content: Primary studies were assessed for methodological quality or bias. GRADE was used to judge certainty in effectiveness findings, and GRADE-CERQual was used to judge confidence in qualitative findings.

document_sections.heading: 2.3.1 Quality assessment of the primary studies included in the reviews
document_sections.content: Eligible randomized trials first underwent research-integrity checks concerning matters such as retraction, registration, ethics and the plausibility of methods and findings. Two reviewers independently assessed bias in trustworthy randomized trials using RoB 2 and in non-randomized trials using ROBINS-I; disagreements were settled by discussion or a third assessor. Randomized-trial assessment considered allocation, recruitment within clusters, departures from intended treatment, missing outcomes, outcome measurement and selective reporting. Non-randomized assessment additionally considered confounding, participant selection and intervention classification. Qualitative studies were appraised with an adapted CASP tool covering study aims, methods, recruitment, collection, analysis, reflexivity, ethics, findings and contribution. Economic studies were assessed using the extended Consensus on Health Economics Criteria list.

document_sections.heading: 2.3.2 Assessment of the certainty of the effectiveness evidence
document_sections.content: GRADE ratings for each effectiveness outcome considered bias, inconsistent results, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. Summary tables presented relative and absolute risks with an overall certainty judgment. The GRADE categories were “high”, indicating strong confidence that the true effect is close to its estimate; “moderate”, indicating that it is probably close but could differ substantially; “low”, indicating limited confidence and a possible substantial difference; and “very low”, indicating very limited confidence and a likely substantial difference.

document_sections.heading: 2.3.3 Assessment of the certainty (confidence) of the qualitative evidence
document_sections.content: GRADE-CERQual assessed each qualitative review finding against methodological limitations, adequacy of data, coherence and relevance. Its “high”, “moderate”, “low” and “very low” ratings respectively indicate that a finding is highly likely, likely, possibly, or not clearly established as a reasonable account of the phenomenon studied.

document_sections.heading: 2.4Formulation of the recommendations
document_sections.content: The Steering Group and ESG prepared outcome summaries and EtD frameworks for each priority question. The GDG considered effects, stakeholder values, resources and cost–effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility and equity, together with the appropriate certainty assessments. Members reviewed materials before deliberating on 31 August and 1 September 2023 and sought consensus. The GDG decided that certainty across these different domains could not be represented adequately by one rating attached to a recommendation; reporting effectiveness certainty alone might misleadingly suggest that other evidence had not been considered. Its recommendation categories were “Recommended”, “Not recommended”, “Recommended only in specific contexts”, “Recommended with monitoring and evaluation”, and “Recommended only in the context of rigorous research”. These distinguish interventions that should be implemented, should not be implemented, apply only in stated circumstances, require monitoring and evaluation, or may be implemented through research that addresses important uncertainties. This classification has been used for WHO MPH recommendations since 2016 across more than 90 individual recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 2.6Decision-making during the GDG meetings
document_sections.content: The GDG discussed supporting evidence and sought agreed wording. Consensus required agreement from three quarters or more of members, provided dissenting members did not strongly oppose it. No member opposed the recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 2.7Document preparation and peer review
document_sections.content: GDG members commented on EtD materials before and during their meeting and reviewed the resulting recommendation document. Five independent external experts subsequently reviewed it. Changes after deliberation and external review were restricted to factual corrections and clarification.

document_sections.heading: 3 Recommendations and supporting evidence
document_sections.content: The GDG made two recommendations, addressing PPH detection and timely standardized treatment. Implementation remarks accompany them. Separate EtD frameworks and findings tables set out the considered benefits and harms, values, resources, cost–effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility and equity.

document_sections.heading: 3.1Recommendations
document_sections.content: Both recommendations are classified “Recommended”. The first concerns routine objective measurement of postpartum blood loss for everyone giving birth. The second concerns objectively assessed blood loss combined with an implementation-supported first-line treatment bundle for women giving birth vaginally. Their remarks qualify how the recommendations should be understood and applied.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 1 Recommended
document_sections.content: For every woman giving birth, routinely measure postpartum blood loss objectively to improve PPH detection and prompt treatment. Objective methods can include calibrated drapes for vaginal births.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 2 Recommended
document_sections.content: For every woman giving birth vaginally, use a prompt, standardized PPH-management approach combining objective blood-loss assessment, a treatment bundle and an implementation strategy. The first-line bundle should rapidly initiate uterine massage, an oxytocic agent, tranexamic acid and intravenous fluids, include genital-tract examination, and provide for escalation of care.

document_sections.heading: Remarks Assessment of postpartum blood loss
document_sections.content: Visual estimation is often inaccurate and can miss PPH until effective intervention is too late; objective quantification is better at identifying it. Most measurement evidence after vaginal birth concerns calibrated drapes. Measurement is especially important during the first few hours after birth, alongside regular checks for warning signs such as tachycardia and hypotension. Measurement and a standardized treatment protocol must operate together: identifying PPH without promptly treating it is unlikely to improve outcomes. Although the available studies involved vaginal births, measuring blood loss at caesarean section is also clinically important. Measurement procedures should preserve women’s customary and cultural needs, including their preferred birth position. Discuss bleeding risks and warning signs throughout the childbirth continuum, including before birth, to support shared decisions. Consider investment in developing and using sustainable, climate-friendly drapes.

document_sections.heading: Care bundle for the treatment of PPH
document_sections.content: The bundle’s individual interventions were already recommended in WHO’s 2012 and 2017 PPH guidance. Here, “bundle” means a clinical-care bundle for PPH treatment. Early PPH detection is integral to first response; much measurement evidence comes from vaginal-birth trials using calibrated drapes. Clinical judgment remains important. In a large trial, the bundle began at measured blood loss of 500 ml or greater, or 300 ml or greater when early warning signs of excessive bleeding were present; these are trial initiation criteria, not a replacement for judgment. That trial paired the bundle with dedicated staffing support, facility audit and feedback, local champions, stocked PPH trolleys or carry cases, and worker training. All bundle interventions should be delivered consistently and promptly, ideally starting within the first 15 minutes after PPH diagnosis. Where some components are unavailable, initiate those available in a timely, standardized way. If bleeding persists despite the entire bundle, promptly escalate to a higher-level facility or a senior clinician capable of further management. Bundle evidence comes chiefly from vaginal-birth trials. There is no clear evidence that its findings would differ at caesarean section, and WHO also recommends the individual interventions for caesarean births, but further research is needed before confidently recommending the bundle for those births. Sustained implementation requires sufficient staff, commodities and stronger health systems at national through district levels. Although supporting studies largely took place in secondary-level facilities, rapid recognition and treatment also matter in primary care, community and home births; those settings need suitable resources, training and adapted implementation. Involving women and communities promotes rights, agency and shared treatment decisions.

document_sections.heading: 4 Dissemination and implementation of the recommendations
document_sections.content: International, national and local stakeholders should consider how to implement the recommendations. Wider access to maternal care and stronger facility capacity are needed for quality care during childbirth. Countries and facilities should incorporate the guidance into appropriate care packages and existing PPH prevention, detection and treatment programmes.

document_sections.heading: 4.1Dissemination and evaluation
document_sections.content: WHO plans a separate executive summary and supporting materials, including a policy brief, updated clinical algorithm and PPH toolkit, to help local adaptation. International and national partners, professional organizations and health authorities will disseminate the guidance; an executive summary is planned in the six United Nations languages. Coordinated international and national action is needed for country-level impact. National and subnational groups should review existing protocols and determine whether they require revision or replacement. In humanitarian emergencies, adaptation should align with other response measures, account for women’s particular needs, values and preferences, and use context-specific tools where needed.

document_sections.heading: 4.2Implementation considerations
document_sections.content: Introducing objective blood-loss measurement and prompt standardized PPH treatment requires planned, participatory local adaptation with relevant stakeholders. Any necessary modification should be justified and documented transparently. Implement both recommendations together within respectful, woman-centred intrapartum and postpartum care and existing PPH programmes. Health systems need current protocols, education and behaviour-change support; reliable supplies of quality medicines, calibrated drapes and equipment; sound procurement, transport and storage; safe disposal of single-use items; and cleaning supplies for reusable tools. Procurement should be limited to quality-certified uterotonics and tranexamic acid. Quality-certified oxytocin should be labelled for storage at 2–8 °C and supplied in single-use ampoules or vials of 10 international units. Room-temperature labelling may not reflect testing under warmer local conditions, and formulation stability differs. Pay particular attention to correct uterotonic dosing and avoiding use for other indications. Reduce the risk of intrathecal tranexamic acid administration, and do not mix it with oxytocin before administration because some tranexamic acid products may interact. Women should receive advance information about PPH prevention and management, possible side-effects and their choices; clear communication with women and their families or companions should also cover bleeding, possible transfer and long-term effects. Personnel need training, supportive supervision and counselling skills, with further monitoring when practice changes and regular competency opportunities where turnover is high. A multicountry trial in secondary-level hospitals with comprehensive emergency obstetric care and on-site surgery showed benefit from standardized, timely detection and bundle treatment. Its active implementation strategy included monthly audit and feedback on detection, bundle use and selected outcomes; trained midwife and doctor champions; regularly replenished PPH trolleys or cases; and on-site simulation and peer-assisted training supported by ward job aids. Staffing must support repeated blood-loss and clinical monitoring, particularly in the first few hours, and coordinated bundle delivery. Adequate personnel, quality commodities and training improve the opportunity to reproduce trial findings. Services may need to review prescribing and administration authority. Reliable, usable information systems can track blood loss, PPH treatment and outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4.3Anticipated impact on the organization of care and resources
document_sections.content: Implementation may entail reorganizing care and reallocating resources, particularly in LMICs. Updated curricula, training and integration into existing childbirth and immediate-postpartum care packages could support implementation and changes in practice. Potential barriers include insufficient skilled personnel, infrastructure, implementation resources, essential supplies, systems for documenting and monitoring practice, and stable staffing when turnover is high.

document_sections.heading: 4.4Monitoring and evaluating guideline implementation
document_sections.content: WHO plans to monitor implementation and effects at service, country and regional levels within broader maternal and newborn quality efforts, using locally aligned input, output and outcome indicators. Country and regional data will be reviewed in the short- to medium-term for effects on national policies; interrupted time series could assess intervention use. For PPH prevention monitoring, WHO recommends prophylactic uterotonic coverage as a process indicator, calculated by dividing women given prophylactic uterotonics during the third stage of labour by all women giving birth. Other locally agreed indicators may be needed for a fuller assessment. WHO guidance also addresses severe-complication quality review through near-miss and criterion-based audits. Monitoring uterotonic quality in low-resource settings may inform the choice of a preventive uterotonic.

document_sections.heading: 5 Research implications
document_sections.content: The GDG prioritized research into the most accurate objective blood-loss measurement methods, including at caesarean section; methods acceptable to women and workers and feasible in practice; measurement for home and community births; outcomes women and families value in PPH detection and treatment; the appropriate bundle after caesarean-section PPH; and ways to sustain bundle use outside research settings.

document_sections.heading: 6 Updating the recommendations
document_sections.content: The Maternal Perinatal Health Guideline Technical Advisory Group will consider these recommendations during its regular reviews of WHO MPH guidance. New evidence with potential to change their basis may prompt an update; without new relevant information, they may instead be revalidated.

document_sections.heading: Annex 2. Priority outcomes used in decisionmaking
document_sections.content: For blood-loss assessment, critical maternal outcomes were accuracy in detecting PPH or severe PPH, defined respectively by ≥ 500 ml and ≥ 1000 ml; postpartum anaemia, defined as Hb lower than 9 mg/dl; and severe morbidity, including coagulopathy, organ failure or intensive-care admission. Important outcomes included blood loss greater than 500 ml, transfusion, plasma expanders, therapeutic uterotonics, changes in heart rate, blood pressure or urine output, additional procedures such as curettage or laparotomy, PPH-related hysterectomy, infection, change in Hb from before to after delivery, maternal death, method-related adverse effects, and maternal and worker satisfaction. For treatment bundles, critical maternal outcomes were death; severe PPH with blood loss ≥ 1000 ml; severe morbidity encompassing intensive-care admission or intubation, end-organ dysfunction or failure, and transfer; transfusion; further blood loss of ≥ 500 ml or ≥ 1000 ml; invasive non-surgical procedures; surgery, including hysterectomy; procedure-related complications; and sepsis. Important maternal outcomes were PPH ≥ 500 ml, mean blood loss in ml, postpartum anaemia, adverse effects including those requiring treatment, other non-surgical interventions, further treatments, artery embolization, delayed breastfeeding, prolonged hospitalization, well-being and satisfaction. Important infant outcomes were neonatal or perinatal death, neonatal intensive-care admission and anaemia in infancy. Health-system outcomes included bundle acceptability, worker adherence, accuracy of blood-loss assessment, time from decision to implementation, medicine and treatment availability, and care costs.
